questions.prompt: Which pattern is associated with feline cognitive dysfunction?

options.text: Disorientation, altered sleep-wake cycles, staring, reduced play, house-soiling, or unprompted nighttime vocalisation.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. These are signs to recognise and report, not a checklist that establishes the diagnosis.

options.text: Only memory loss that can be demonstrated with a formal home test.
options.feedback: The owner-facing evidence describes observable behavioural patterns, not a home memory examination.

options.text: Any one new senior behaviour, regardless of duration or context.
options.feedback: A single change can deserve observation, but association depends on pattern and still cannot replace clinical rule-out.

questions.prompt: Why is cognitive dysfunction described as a rule-out diagnosis?

options.text: Every senior cat must be tested for every possible disease before any household observation is recorded.
options.feedback: The log comes first as evidence for the conversation. The veterinary team determines the appropriate rule-out process.

options.text: The condition has no observable signs, so owners should ignore behaviour and wait for imaging.
options.feedback: Observable signs are useful for recognition and reporting. They are insufficient for diagnosis, not irrelevant.

options.text: Arthritis, kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, hypertension, periodontal disease, and neurological causes can produce overlapping signs.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Clinical examination and testing are needed before the cognitive explanation can be confirmed.

questions.prompt: What is the Chapter 3 medical-first callback in this context?

options.text: Use whichever earlier chapter gives the most familiar explanation and treat that as the cause.
options.feedback: The point of the callback is that overlapping signs keep several explanations open, not that one earlier chapter wins.

options.text: Recognise the behavioural signature, report the full pattern, and avoid privately settling on one cause.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. The owner notices and escalates while diagnosis remains a clinical rule-out process.

options.text: Ignore house-soiling because it has already been taught and cannot mean something new in senior life.
options.feedback: The same observation can have different causes at different times. Earlier learning makes the report richer, not the sign irrelevant.

questions.prompt: How should owner-support suggestions be used after assessment?

options.text: Implement every item uniformly so care remains fair across households.
options.feedback: Uniform completeness ignores the financial, time, emotional, and physical budgets that make a plan sustainable.

options.text: Discuss relevant supports with the vet and scale feasible changes to the household's real budgets.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Environmental support and caregiver capacity belong together rather than in competing lists.

options.text: Choose an online diet or supplement first because environmental changes take longer.
options.feedback: Diet and medication decisions remain vet-led after rule-out. Speed does not make self-selected treatment appropriate.

questions.prompt: Milo wanders at night, sleeps at different times, and has one accident. Home checks show no dental or mobility change. What next?

options.text: Wait indefinitely because none of the signs is an immediate emergency.
options.feedback: This confuses urgency with relevance. A persistent unexplained cluster warrants a professional conversation even when not emergent.

options.text: Start cognitive support because the two most obvious alternatives appear absent.
options.feedback: Many alternatives cannot be ruled out at home, and treatment or supplements should not precede the vet-led process.

options.text: Bring the full positive and negative pattern to the vet because clinical causes remain unexcluded.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Clear home checks improve the report but do not replace bloodwork, blood pressure, examination, or other clinical assessment.

questions.prompt: A senior cat yowls at night, eats less, and has newly bad breath. Which report is most useful?

options.text: Report only the yowling because cognitive signs are the oldest cat's most likely issue.
options.feedback: Selecting only signs that fit the first hypothesis creates confirmation bias and hides a relevant dental observation.

options.text: Report all three together and identify bad breath as a dental warning that challenges a cognitive-only explanation.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. The complete cluster gives the vet a plausible alternative to investigate without asking the owner to diagnose it.

options.text: Treat the breath change separately because dental and cognitive signs cannot share a cause.
options.feedback: The evidence does not justify separating them. Painful eating or oral discomfort could plausibly relate to appetite and vocal change.

questions.prompt: Which response avoids both cognitive-specific failure modes?

options.text: Wait for a dramatic crisis so the household cannot be accused of overreacting.
options.feedback: That is normalisation drift and under-reaction, not a balanced response to persistent behavioural change.

options.text: Request cognitive medication immediately so the vet can decide whether to refuse it.
options.feedback: That begins with a treatment conclusion and skips the rule-out process the consultation is meant to support.

options.text: Record and raise gradual change without calling it 'just old,' while withholding diagnosis and products until rule-out.
options.feedback: This is the best synthesis. It acts on evidence without closing the case before clinical assessment.
